This document defines a DataEncoding: a mapping of the OPC UA type model onto Apache Arrow, a PubSub batch mapping and a historian access surface. It defines no OPC UA information model of its own: it has no NodeSet, no ObjectTypes, no VariableTypes, no DataTypes, no ReferenceTypes and no Instances. The NodeClass clauses of OPC 20020 are therefore omitted rather than left empty, and Annex A states the generated per-type reference this document does define in place of a NodeSet.

runs.text: Apache Arrow is a columnar in-memory format: the values of one field are stored together rather than each record being stored whole. Analytical work reads a few fields of many records, and a columnar layout lets it touch only those fields, in a form a processor can scan without decoding value by value. The same layout is what Arrow puts on the wire, so a reader consumes it without parsing.

OPC UA moves data one record at a time, which suits control and does not suit analysis. A historian answering "the last month of these forty signals" returns a great many small structures, each carrying its own field identities, and every consumer then reshapes them into columns before it can do anything useful.

This document defines an Arrow DataEncoding for OPC UA, a PubSub mapping that publishes batches of DataSet messages as record batches, and an access surface that returns the result of a historian read as a stream of record batches rather than as individual values.
Arrow is for the work OPC UA record-at-a-time delivery serves badly: reading many values of a few signals, and handing them to something that analyses rather than controls.

Historian and analytics. A query for a month of a few dozen signals returns as a stream of record batches, in the layout an analytical engine already uses, so the consumer neither parses each value nor reshapes rows into columns before it can begin.

High-rate PubSub. A publisher that would otherwise emit a message per sample emits a batch covering an interval, which amortises the header and the framing over many samples and keeps the columnar layout intact end to end.

Interchange with the wider data ecosystem. The encoded form is consumed directly by tools that already speak Arrow, without an intermediate conversion that would have to be written, maintained and trusted.
Arrow is not a replacement for the OPC UA binary encoding in the request-response path, where a single value is wanted at once and a columnar layout has nothing to amortise over.
